analysis.one_liner: Repeals major parts of the Affordable Care Act and cuts taxes on high-income households and health industries.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 217-213 on May 4, 2017, but the Senate never voted on final passage, and the bill died on the Senate calendar when that Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced much of the Affordable Care Act. It ends the individual and employer coverage penalties, repeals the income-based premium subsidies after 2019 and replaces them with smaller age-based tax credits, and caps federal Medicaid funding while ending the ACA's Medicaid expansion in 2020. It also repeals taxes that fall mainly on high earners and on health insurers, drug makers, and medical device makers. The House passed it by a nearly party-line 217-213 vote, but the Senate, after opening debate on a 51-50 vote broken by the Vice President, never brought it to a final vote and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most directly: the bill repeals the 3.8% net investment income tax and the additional Medicare tax, both of which apply only above high income thresholds, and it raises health savings account limits. Health insurers gain from repeal of their annual market-share fee and from a provision allowing them to deduct executive pay above $500,000; brand-name drug makers gain repeal of their annual fee, and medical device makers gain repeal of the device excise tax. People buying their own insurance would get a new refundable age-based tax credit starting in 2020, capped at $14,000 per family, and states would receive a Patient and State Stability Fund for high-risk pools, premium stabilization, and mental health and maternity services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, insurers, drug and device makers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable, advanceable age-based tax credit beginning in 2020 for people buying individual health insurance, capped at $14,000 per family and based on age and income.

Appropriates a Patient and State Stability Fund — $15 billion in each of 2018 and 2019 and $10 billion a year through 2026 — for high-risk individuals, premium stabilization, maternity care, and mental health or substance use treatment, plus $15 billion for a federal reinsurance-style program and $8 billion for states that let premiums vary by health status.
Increases community health center funding by $422 million for fiscal year 2017 and preserves disproportionate share hospital payments for hospitals serving many low-income patients.
Repeals the individual mandate penalty and the employer mandate penalty, and allows taxpayers to deduct unreimbursed medical expenses above 5.8% of income instead of 10%.
Expands health savings accounts, including higher contribution limits and joint catch-up contributions for married couples.

analysis.who_pays: Lower-income people lose the most: the income-based premium subsidies are repealed after 2019 in favor of smaller age-based credits, cost-sharing reductions for low-income plans end after 2019, and federal Medicaid funding is capped per enrollee starting in fiscal 2020 while the ACA Medicaid expansion is eliminated, with only enrollees continuously enrolled kept covered. Older adults can be charged up to five times what young adults pay, up from three times, and in states that take waivers, premiums could vary by health status. Anyone with a gap in coverage of more than 62 days faces a 30% premium surcharge for one year. Medicaid adds work requirements for nondisabled adults and ends retroactive coverage, and for one year no federal funds may go to family planning providers like Planned Parenthood.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicaid recipients, older and sicker buyers

drawbacks.text: Federal Medicaid funding becomes a per-enrollee cap beginning in fiscal 2020, with states that exceed their target getting reduced federal funding the next year, shifting the risk of recessions, epidemics, or higher health costs onto states and patients.

The income-based premium subsidies are repealed after 2019 and replaced with age-based credits, and cost-sharing reductions for low-income people end after 2019, so help would be smaller for people with low incomes and larger for higher-income buyers.

States may apply for waivers to drop the essential health benefits requirement and to let premiums vary by age up to 5-to-1 — and under the passed version, to vary premiums by health status — which could raise costs for older people and those with preexisting conditions, cushioned by only $8 billion in transition aid.

The bill repeals the 3.8% net investment income tax and the additional Medicare tax, both of which apply only to incomes above high thresholds, and repeals taxes on health insurers, branded drug makers, and medical devices.

The bill ends the essential health benefits requirement for Medicaid alternative benefit plans after 2019, eliminates up to three months of retroactive Medicaid coverage, and lets states lower the income threshold for children's Medicaid eligibility.
For one year, federal funds may not be paid to family planning providers such as Planned Parenthood, cutting off a source of care for some patients.

Defenders argued the bill restored state flexibility, ended a federal mandate to buy insurance, and slowed federal health spending; the honest cost is that the spending reduction comes largely by shifting costs to states, older adults, and people with low incomes, while the tax relief is concentrated on high earners and the health industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill contains real help for some people — age-based tax credits for individual-market buyers, a large state stability fund, and expanded health savings accounts. But the largest and most certain effects run the other way: substantial tax cuts that go mainly to high-income households and to insurers, drug makers, and device makers, paid for in part by capping Medicaid, phasing out the expansion, and shrinking subsidies for low-income buyers. Older adults and people with health problems in waiver states would face higher premiums. As designed, the gains and losses fall on very different groups — the tax cuts on the affluent, the coverage losses on the poor and the sick — which is why the bill drew universal Democratic opposition and 20 Republican defections in the House, and why it never found the votes in a Republican-controlled Senate.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 217-213 in May 2017, but the Senate never took a final vote — after opening debate on a 51-50 tie-break vote, it rejected every Democratic motion and then returned the bill to the calendar, where it sat until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Committee on the Budget reported the bill as an original measure on March 20, 2017, and the House passed it on May 4, 2017, by a recorded vote of 217 to 213.
No Democrat voted for the bill in the House; all 193 Democrats voted no, along with 20 of the 238 Republicans.
The Senate received the bill on June 7, 2017, and placed it on the Senate calendar.

On July 25, 2017, the Senate agreed to a motion to proceed by a 51-50 vote, with the Vice President casting the tie-breaking vote; every Democrat and Independent opposed it and two Republicans joined them.
On July 26-28, 2017, the Senate rejected four Democratic motions to commit the bill to committee — the procedural votes that would have sent it to committee for changes — all along party lines.
On July 28, 2017, the Senate returned the bill to the calendar. No Senator ever cast a vote on passage, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who get coverage through Medicaid and the ACA marketplaces kept the existing system, since the Medicaid caps, expansion repeal, and subsidy changes never took effect. High-income households, health insurers, and drug and device makers did not receive the tax repeals the bill contained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicaid and ACA marketplace enrollees kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: House passage was 217-213 with zero of 193 Democrats and 20 of 238 Republicans in favor; every Senate vote — the 51-50 motion to proceed broken by the Vice President and four 43-57 to 48-52 rejections of Democratic motions — fell entirely along party lines.

industries.note: The bill repeals the annual fee on health insurers based on market share and repeals the rule barring them from deducting executive pay above $500,000, while ending the cost-sharing subsidies their customers relied on and replacing them with smaller age-based credits and state-run stabilization payments. Their tax burden falls and they become the channel for public stabilization money as consumer protections and subsidies shrink.
Repeals the annual fee on branded prescription pharmaceutical manufacturers, one of the ACA's financing taxes, saving the industry money with no offsetting benefit to patients.
Repeals the ACA's medical device excise tax in its entirety, removing a financing tax on the industry.

Repeals the 3.8% net investment income tax on individuals, estates, and trusts above high income thresholds and the additional Medicare tax on high wages — the two most heavily progressive taxes in the ACA. The revenue loss is a direct tax cut concentrated at the top.

The bill eliminates scheduled Medicaid disproportionate share (DSH) payment cuts and adds safety-net funding for non-expansion states, but caps and cuts Medicaid itself, leaving hospitals facing more uninsured patients and less federal support over time.
Repeals the ACA's 10% excise tax on indoor tanning services; a small, direct benefit to the industry and its customers.
